newsitem.title: POLAND: Cash squeeze lifts Polish zloty to six-month peak.
newsitem.headline: Cash squeeze lifts Polish zloty to six-month peak.

text.p: Poland's zloty hit a six-month high against its basket of currencies on Tuesday as banks sold the currencies to gain liquidity before pre-Christmas cash outlows tighten the money market in late December, analysts said.
"The zloty's rise is in large part caused by the cash shortage on the money market and lack of liquidity on the forex market," said Andrzej Ladko, chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Since Monday, the zloty has firmed about half a percentage point against the basket of currencies and by 1130 GMT on Tuesday, was trading at 2.65 percent from the parity rate.
The zloty was at 2.8635/45 to the dollar and at 1.8293/98 to the mark at midday, while dollar/mark traded at 1.5650.

"Banks can either gain liquidity by buying zlotys near the lombard rate (of 25 percent) or shortening foreign currency exposure. So, its no wonder they chose to sell dollars," said Tomasz Zysko, senior forex dealer at BDK SA.

Analysts said the zloty may remain bullish until the end of 1996 as several foreign banks in Poland were expected to increase their captial before year end, adding at least $100 million to the already currency-heavy market.
They said that in the last several months whenever the zloty strengthened, foreign investors knocked it down by selling Polish treasuries to take profits.
Now, however, foreigers no longer have large amounts of Polish bills.

"Most foreign investors already cut Polish portfolios as the interest alone does not give enough carry without capital gains created by zloty appreciation," said one emerging markets dealer at an investment bank in London.
Analysts said a boom in lending to the non-financial sector, which grew 3.1 percent in the first 20 days of November and by nearly 35 percent since January, also stirred demand for zlotys.

Analysts said even small amounts could move the forex market as only a few investors were active and did not close the majority of their intraday positions at the the post-trade fixing with the central bank.
"The market is very shallow, and whenever you have a situation that there are only several active players, small sums can move the zloty by a figure or more," one dealer at a large Polish bank said.

In the longer term, the zloty's fate remains unclear an expected widening of the current account deficit in 1997 is set to battle against privatisation and foreign direct investment inflows to shape the zloty's course next year.
"Logic would suggest that a widening current account gap should weaken the zloty next year, but the Polish market has often defied logic in the past," Handlowy's Ladko said.
